title: Commercial Turf in Northeast Florida | TIMELESS Grass & Greens
description: Commercial turf from Fernandina Beach to St. Augustine Shores, planned around county landscape codes, stormwater permits and city turf rules. Free estimate.
h1: Turf for your courtyard, dog run or play area, planned around local code.
lede: Put turf in a courtyard, dog run or play area on business or shared property from Fernandina Beach to St. Augustine Shores. Here your county or city code and the site’s stormwater permit set the terms, so check both early. Then book a free visit for a custom layout and written price.
wins: A courtyard, dog run or play area with no mowing
Required planting kept on the plan, with turf beside it
Stormwater permit questions settled before the base goes in

answer.question: Does Florida’s synthetic turf law cover commercial property?
answer.answer: No. DEP’s FAQ says Rule 62-308.100 applies only to single-family residential properties of 1 acre or less, not to condominiums, parks or commercial properties. The limits section 125.572 puts on local rules are tied to DEP’s standards for single-family residential property. On a commercial site, your county or city code and any stormwater permit set the terms. Call 303-349-2368 for a free estimate.

blocks.h2: The state turf rule leaves your site to local code.
paras: The statewide shield against local turf bans isn’t built for your site. Under section 125.572 of the 2026 Florida Statutes, a city or county can’t ban turf that meets DEP’s standards for single-family residential property, or regulate turf inconsistently with those standards. On a restaurant patio, office courtyard or daycare yard, don’t count on it to override a stricter county or city rule.

The home-lot standards don’t carry over on their own either. Rule 62-308.100, in effect since 19 May 2026, is a set of minimum standards local governments must use, and DEP’s FAQ says the department runs no permit, inspection or enforcement program under it. Ask the reviewing office which turf standards, if any, it applies to your site. Our Florida turf rules guide covers the home-lot standard.

blocks.h2: Ask whether the turf area changes a stormwater permit.
paras: Florida’s Rule 62-330.020 requires an environmental resource permit for work that adds up to more than 4,000 square feet of impervious and semi-impervious surface used by vehicles, more than 9,000 square feet of it in total, or a project area over five acres. It also covers work in wetlands or other surface waters, work that’s part of a larger common plan of development, and any change to a project already permitted. The rule’s carve-outs include listed exemptions, grandfathered projects, routine maintenance of a permitted project that isn’t being altered, and the 10/2 general permit for upland stormwater systems.

The St. Johns River Water Management District’s Applicant’s Handbook, Volume I, dated June 28, 2024, defines impervious as surfaces that don’t let water through, or barely do. Semi-impervious means surfaces that partly restrict it, such as gravel, limerock and certain compacted soils. Neither definition names artificial turf, so ask the District how it will count the turf and its stone base before you set a budget.

If the site was built under a stormwater permit, the handbook lists adding more than 10 percent or 0.5 acres of impervious and semi-impervious surface, whichever is less, as one factor that makes a modification more than minor, unless the original permit already allowed enough treatment and flood capacity for the change. Bring the permit number, the approved drainage plan and the turf product’s drainage data to that conversation before the grass comes out. Our impervious surface guide lists the questions to ask.

blocks.h2: Required planting stays planting. Turf goes beside it.
paras: Two county codes say so outright. In unincorporated Clay County, Sec. 18.5-53 says synthetic or artificial turf can’t be used in place of the required plants, and Sec. 18.5-51 applies those standards to the paved ground areas of all nonresidential buildings. In unincorporated Nassau County, Sec. 37.05 says synthetic or artificial trees, shrubs, groundcovers or vines are not acceptable substitutes.

Whether a code reaches a finished site depends on the work. Nassau’s section covers all new development. A site built under earlier landscaping rules doesn’t have to meet it unless you redevelop, reconfigure, expand or change the use, and even then not if the site has 7,500 square feet of impervious area or less and adds no more than 750, or has more and adds less than 2,000 square feet and less than 10 percent of the existing impervious area. In Jacksonville, Sec. 656.1209 covers new landscapes, and reaches an existing commercial site once renovations within two years total at least 60 percent of the assessed value of the lot improvements, or the building’s square footage grows by 60 percent. Sec. 656.1217 requires an approved landscape plan before any building or paving permit is issued.

In unincorporated St. Johns County, LDC Section 6.06.02.A.5 (January 12, 2026) lets rocks, gravel and mulch sit with living plants and says artificial plants can’t meet any landscaping requirement. It doesn’t name turf, so ask Development Review, which handles commercial plan review, how it applies that line to your plan. The county’s impervious surface definition (June 2, 2026) lists buildings, concrete, pools, wet retention and detention areas, and pavement or compacted materials used for parking or roadways. Turf isn’t named there either.

If your St. Johns site was built under approved construction plans, ask whether turf counts as a change to them. Section 13.16 of the county’s construction plans manual, revised May 2026, says changes to approved plans need Development Review approval before they go in the field. A change that significantly alters the drainage or site plan goes through the same process as a new project.

blocks.h2: In Atlantic Beach, the base gets inspected first.
paras: Cities can set their own terms. Atlantic Beach’s turf installation guidelines (undated, online as of September 2026) apply to all artificial turf installations. They call for a turf system rated at 100 inches per hour or more over at least 4 inches of free-draining stone, with product specifications, permeability test results, installation details and a site plan for review. The city inspects the stone base before turf covers it.

If your site has a retention area, plan around it. The guidelines allow turf in a privately owned retention or drainage area only if the basin keeps its designed storage and function, with drainage structures, overflow paths and maintenance access left clear. The city may ask for engineering documentation that stormwater capacity and drainage still work. Elsewhere, treat turf inside a permitted stormwater system as a question for the reviewing office and the District first.

blocks.h2: Bring the site’s permits to the free visit.
paras: Bring the parcel address, the approved site plan, the landscape plan the property was built under and any stormwater permit number. Mark the required planting, retention areas, swales and drainage structures. We measure the area, check the ground and draw a custom layout you approve before work starts, then give you a written price.

If a reviewer wants product specifications, drainage data or a base cross-section, agree who gathers and submits them before you set a start date. See the commercial turf service for surface options, and the northeast Florida page for everything else we install here.

faq.q: A community development district or association manages our space. Does the state law help?
faq.a: No. DEP’s FAQ says the rule doesn’t address HOA requirements or deed restrictions. And since 1 July 2026, Ch. 2026-164 says section 125.572’s limits on local rules don’t apply when a community development district enforces deed restrictions. Get the district’s or association’s written approval, and check the county or city code for the parcel too. Our Florida HOA guide covers the association side.

faq.q: Does Florida’s rubber infill limit apply to our play area?
faq.a: No. The limit to natural infill such as sand, rock or shell, with rubber or synthetic infill only within the footprint of playground equipment, is part of the home-lot rule. Choose the infill for how the space is used, and ask the reviewing office whether local code sets its own terms.
